sweep_summary: Limbu is not in the catalog. Both title-hit items are Hildebrandt's Autotyp word-domains study: the 2007 Himalayan Linguistics paper (open access, already on file, read and verified) and its 2004 ICSTLL Lund talk (unpublished, no copy online, superseded by 2007). Hildebrandt 2007: 14-16 states, with van Driem 1987: 15 as primary source, that Limbu has a single weak, non-distinctive main stress on the verbal stem/root to the exclusion of prefixes and suffixes (e.g. ['tʰaŋˌŋaŋˌŋã:], [kɛ'siraˌdhaŋˌˌŋi:]), that a bare prefix+stem word stresses the prefix (['kuˌla:p]), and that secondary stress falls on non-initial bimoraic trochaic feet (p. 8). Michailovsky 2002: ix (Mewa Khola dialect) corroborates: roots accented, prefixes and suffixes unaccented. van Driem 1987 (DOI 10.1515/9783110846812, ISBN 9783110112825, phonology ch. pp. 1-19) remains paywalled; not in HathiTrust, Google Books and de Gruyter blocked from our machine; its p. 15 wording is known only via Hildebrandt. Weidert & Subba 1985 Rosetta excerpts (two newly saved), Tumbahang 2007 (Chhatthare) and LSI Sikkim 2009 are silent on stress placement. in updated with a dated sweep note. work relied on web lookups/curl and on-disk material.

[...] Note that in example (21) the stem still bears the single main stress, to the exclusion of the prefix. [...] This indicates that prefixes never bear main stress [...] in almost all cases, main stress falls on the stem, with optional secondary stress occurring on non-initial syllables, depending on foot structure [...] In such cases where the word consists exclusively of a prefix and stem, the main stress will fall on the prefix, thus avoiding an iambic rhythm of weak-strong, which is unattested in Kiranti languages in general (Bickel 2003b).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Limbu has one weak, non-contrastive main stress per word, located on the (first syllable of the) stem/root; prefixes and suffixes are unstressed, so stress is word-initial in unprefixed words and non-initial after a prefix. Exception: in words consisting only of prefix + monosyllabic stem (e.g. ku-la:p 'its wing') main stress shifts to the prefix, giving a trochee. Independently corroborated first-hand by Michailovsky 2002: ix ('prefixes and suffixes are unaccented... roots, which are accented').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Feet are bimoraic trochees; 'a secondary stress is found on all non-initial feet' (p. 8), surfacing only when a post-stem suffix/clitic is bimoraic and follows a consonant (with gemination, e.g. [a'njumˌme:]); light monomoraic suffix strings stay unfooted and unstressed.
new_statements.exceptions: Prefix + bare stem words take main stress on the prefix (['kuˌla:p]); van Driem (1987:15, as quoted) calls stress 'not very pronounced and non-distinctive'; Michailovsky 2002: xi notes some nouns syncopate their first syllable after a possessive prefix and others do not, 'possibly because of an accentual difference'.
new_statements.domain_note: Grammatical/phonological word (stem plus affixes and enclitics); Hildebrandt's transcriptions come from connected-speech LACITO recordings (Mewa Khola texts) plus van Driem's Phedappe citation forms; main-stress domain = prefix+stem, other P-word diagnostics = stem+suffixes.
new_statements.identity_note: Hildebrandt 2007 combines van Driem's Phedappe-dialect data (Tehrathum) with her own transcriptions of LACITO/Pangloss recordings of the Maiwa-Mewa Khola (Taplejung, 'Taplejunge/Tamarkhole') dialect; Michailovsky 2002 describes the Mewa Khola dialect. Tumbahang 2007 (silent on stress) describes Chhatthare Limbu, a divergent southern variety sometimes treated as a separate language but filed under limb1266 in Glottolog's bibliography. All fall under language-level limb1266.

new_statements.reading: Limbu has one weak, non-contrastive main stress per word, located on the lexical stem/root regardless of its position (initial in unprefixed words, non-initial after prefixes); prefixes and suffixes are unstressed except that a bare prefix+stem word shifts main stress to the prefix to avoid an iamb. Secondary stress falls on non-initial bimoraic (trochaic) feet, which only form on heavy tautomorphemic suffixes after a consonant. Coding suggestion: morphologically governed root stress (not positional); Michailovsky 2002: ix independently states roots accented, affixes unaccented.

sources.note: Sec. 3.2-3.4 (pp. 8-16): single main stress per word falls on the (verbal/nominal) stem; prefixes never bear main stress except in words consisting only of prefix+stem, where main stress falls on the prefix (avoiding an iamb); bimoraic trochaic feet with secondary stress on non-initial feet (evidenced by gemination and small-scale acoustic data from LACITO recordings); quotes van Driem 1987:15 that stress is 'not very pronounced and is non-distinctive'.

sources.quote: In open (vowel-ending) syllables, length is generally determined by word accent and other factors: for example, prefixes and suffixes are unaccented and rather short compared to roots, which are accented. [p. ix] ... Other words, like nara 'face', do not undergo syncopation, possibly because of an accentual difference. [p. xi]

sources.note: Maiwa-Mewa dialect: roots are accented, prefixes and suffixes unaccented; accent conditions vowel length in open syllables and possibly syncopation. Agrees with Hildebrandt 2007 (stress on the root/stem).
